cards.explanation: The answer is the heavens. The writer says we have “…a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God…” The other high priests in this passage are appointed from among men. This one passed through the heavens, friends.

The answer is to hold firmly to what we profess. The writer says, “…let us hold firmly to what we profess.” He says it because we already have this great high priest. Think of grabbing a hot tray with a thin oven mitt, friends. You don't loosen up, you hold on.

The answer is False. The writer says, “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses…” So our high priest is able to sympathize, friends. The writer goes on to say He “…was tempted in every way that we are…”
The answer is that He was without sin. The verse says He “…was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin.” Every way, and still without sin, bakers. That little word “yet” carries a lot.

The answer is with confidence. The writer says, “Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence…” No tiptoeing, no sneaking in the back, friends. It's a throne of grace, so you can walk up like you belong.

The answer is mercy. The verse says we approach “…so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need.” Mercy and grace, both on offer, bakers. And the help comes in our time of need, which is when we want it most.

The answer is True. The writer says, “Every high priest is appointed from among men to represent them in matters relating to God…” So he comes from the people he stands in front of, friends. He's one of them, picked to represent them.

The answer is sacrifices. The verse says a high priest is appointed “…to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.” Gifts and sacrifices, that's the job, bakers. And it's for sins, which is the heavy part of the verse.

The answer is that he is subject to weakness himself. The writer says, “He is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is subject to weakness.” The reason is right there in the verse, friends. He knows weakness from the inside, so he can be gentle.

The answer is False. The writer says the high priest “…is obligated to offer sacrifices for his own sins, as well as for the sins of the people.” That's two lists, friends, and his own name is on one of them. It fits with what the writer just said about him being subject to weakness.

The answer is that he must be called by God. The writer says, “No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God…” So the honor is given, not grabbed, friends. Nobody gets this one by being the first in line.
The answer is Aaron. The writer says a high priest “…must be called by God, just as Aaron was.” Aaron is the high priest the writer points to as an example, bakers. Called, not self-appointed.

The answer is False. The writer says, “So also Christ did not take upon Himself the glory of becoming a high priest, but He was called…” He didn't take it, friends. He was called, the same way the writer said a high priest receives the honor.

The answer is False. The text has God saying, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” Forever doesn't hit a limit at the end of His earthly life, friends. Back in Genesis 14:18, Melchizedek appears as king of Salem and priest of God Most High.

The answer is death. The writer says Jesus prayed “…to the One who could save Him from death…” I think this one hurts a little, friends. The writer says it plainly, and it comes with loud cries and tears.
The answer is True. The writer says, “…and He was heard because of His reverence.” Loud cries and tears, and He was heard, friends. The text says it plainly.
The answer is because of His reverence. The writer says, “…and He was heard because of His reverence.” The verse gives that one reason and no other, bakers. Reverence is the word the writer picks.

The answer is suffered. The writer says, “Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered.” That's a surprising line, friends, and I won't dress it up. The verse says suffered, and that's the word.
The answer is all who obey Him. The writer says, “…He became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him” That's who the verse names, friends. All who obey Him.
